In a nutshell:

GamerGate is a scandal involving unethical conduct amongst video game journalists (including, amongst other things, failing to disclose relationships they have with developers/publishers and failing to label certain forms of paid advertising content as such in order to distinguish it from independently-written content).

Kotaku is one of several websites whose employees are involved in the scandal; other notable examples include Gamasutra, Polygon, Rock Paper Shotgun, and Destructoid.

A few resources to get you started:

  • GamerGate in 60 Seconds
  • If It's Not About Ethics...
  • Chris von Csefalvay's four-part analysis of the GamerGate Twitter network (which debunks the oft-reported claim that GamerGate is about harassment and discrimination); One, Two, Three, Four
  • GamerGate Press Dossier - archive.is backup
  • Know Your Meme: GamerGate

Now, to expand on the above... the seeds of the scandal had been planted long before the events in 2014 that caused it to erupt.

For example, there were incidents like these:

  • The firing of Jeff Gerstmann (allegedly for writing a negative review of Kane & Lynch: Dead Men)
  • The whole Shadow of Mordor debacle (where the publisher - Warner Brothers Interactive, IIRC - tried to insert punitive clauses into YouTube review contracts; IIRC, they boiled down to "if you publish a negative review after signing this contract, we get to sue your pants off")
  • The smear campaign against Brad Wardell, CEO of Stardock Games, which deliberately mischaracterized a (since resolved) legal battle against a former employee who - if memory serves - was both fired and taken to court for gross misconduct and incompetence; said employee unsuccessfully countersued, claiming discrimination, retaliation, and sexual harassment
  • A very similar smear campaign against Max Temkin, creator of Cards Against Humanity, which involved since-disproven allegations of sexual assault
  • And last, but not least, the infamous DoritosGate incident of 2012, which spawned the whole "Geoff Keighley, Dorito Pope" meme.

GamerGate essentially started out as something that would normally have died in a week. One amateur developer with no development experience released a text based game built using a build-your-own-game type engine. She received an unusual amount of attention from the games media. It was surprisingly mentioned multiple times on Kotaku. One of their reporters even went out of his way to mention it on another site as well. A jilted ex of said developer then publishes a lengthy letter about the breakdown of their relationship. In particular he suggests, and provides some evidence indicating, that she was intimately involved with numerous individuals in the games media including the reporter who mentioned her multiple times.

Keep in mind that the games media has an absolutely horrific reputation. Controversy there is nothing unusual or shocking. For instance Jeff Gerstmann was the editorial director of GameSpot. He was fired for giving (and allowing) "too low" of game scores from companies that were advertising their games on GameSpot. These includes scores such as 7.5/10. That was a huge deal among gamers and then dead a few weeks later. Somebody supposedly getting some free coverage for supposed favors or relationships pales in comparison.

Things only get interesting here when the developer in question starts everything rolling by filing a fraudulent DMCA takedown on a video that was discussing these issues. This resulted in a boost in discussion on the topic and an increased trending of the ultimately eponymous GamerGate twitter hashtag, but it was still relatively obscure. Ultimately somebody asked a far more well known YouTuber, TotalBiscuit, his opinion on the matter. He stated that he'd never heard about this but particular issue but mentioned he strongly opposed censorship if the fraudulent DMCA takedown was indeed true, and felt the games media in general was suffering from a widespread lack of ethics and integrity. You can read his post here. His response was shared on Reddit here. That thread in /r/games is what effectively created GamerGate. There were tens of thousands of comments. The mods there decided to delete them all. Here is a web archive of the thread that you can catch some of the comments in before they get deleted. It was a Streisand Effect of epic proportions.

Suddenly GamerGate and related issues were being discussed everywhere related to gaming. The media, which was strongly under fire, reacted in two ways. On one front they worked to paint as vile a picture of GamerGate as they possibly could. Take the most offensive and overt troll, and then claim he's not only a genuine GamerGate supporter but a typical example. On the other front there was a massive campaign of censorship on the games media's discussion boards. Any discussion of GamerGate or journalistic ethics was censored on the sites in question as well as on some third party sites. It was a coordinated attack designed to discredit the movement before it got any larger.

The mods on Reddit got in on this as well and GamerGate discussion was actively censored on most of the larger subs. /r/KotakuInAction is one of the refuges that many folks just looking to discuss these issues ended up at. You can read an archive of its posts from the first days here. KiA It's a sub that went from brand new to averaging more than 600,000 unique visitors a month seemingly overnight. Even the early posts make it clear the media portrayal of GamerGate is about as accurate and unbiased as their portrayal of Clinton. That in a nutshell is a brief history and how it turned into a media vs gamer battle.

Here's what I know about it, from watching it unfold first hand:

It started with some low level drama over a game called Depression Quest made by game developer Zoe Quinn (who many people call an SJW and who appeared at the UN recently to talk about 'cyber violence'). The game was more of a choose your own adventure novel, was very low effort and it got a lot of hate and people wanted it removed from steam. Despite this, there was a lot of good press for the game, defending the game and Quinn and shunning those who dare oppose it.

This is when the 'Quinnspiracy' theories began, and people started noticing links between Quinn and certain journalists. The general theory was that she slept with people who then gave her good reviews. This spiraled further when an insane amount of game journalism outlets all posted articles about the same thing ("The death of gamers", essentially about how the identity of gamers as angry, bigoted and sexist is coming to an end). This was what convinced people that games journalists were colluding and corrupt (of which I believe there is an awful lot of evidence).

The problem is that gamergate isn't so self contained. Whilst many people centered it on gaming journalism and integrity (which is where the name gamergate came from), it was to a larger degree about SJW's. Many people who 'supported' gamergate (that is to say, believe that gaming journalism is corrupt) were also very much against SJW's who they saw as hijacking the industry, putting in token gay, transexual or female characters that didn't add to games. A lot of gaming journalist outlets would parrot these views, and so these people believed an agenda was being pushed by people who had influence over journalists. Because of this, those 'against' gamergate were mainly SJW's and those who saw gamergate as a racist/sexist/homophobic movement. There was an awful lot of dumb rhetoric and vitriol spewed by both sides (and countless amounts of doxxing and harassment, again on both sides) and generally the whole thing is a toxic mess. Because of this, it's very hard to discuss the topic without it blowing up. Some people think if you support gamergate, then you're a bigot, whilst others believe if you're against it, you're an SJW. It's very hard to touch the topic without attracting hate (I know total biscuit, when commenting on gamergate in the early days, said it was like a blunderbuss of hate that would fire in every direction).

What's always saddened me is that in the mess, a lot of information/events were buried. What I remember is that Zoe Quinn posted on twitter about people on wizard chan 'harassing' her by complaining about the game, and so her followers raided the place. In reality there was about two posts about who depression quest sucked. It's worth pointing out that wizard chan is a site dedicated to lonely virgins, and it was just kind of sad that Quinn would manufacture hate against it like that to get sympathy and publicity.

At the same time, it's understandable why someone would be against gamergate. The mainstream opinion pumped out by gaming journalists was that it was a bigoted movement that harassed people, and if that's all you knew about it, you'd think it was horrible. It's a damn shame, and the whole event has really tarnished the games industry. I've read interviews of anonymous game developers who say it's made them sacred to discuss certain topics with fans because they're in the shadow of that vitriolic mess, and that it'd be all too easy for someone spiteful to dox or harass them.

Gamergate beginnings - It started when a bloke named Eron Gjoni made a rambling screed about his abusive ex girlfriend Zoe Quinn. In that screed he mentioned Ms. Quinn cheated on him with a games journalist name Nathan Grayson (along with 4 other people in the industry). Grayson wrote about Quinn's game before, so there's an obvious ethical issue. No gaming website would cover it and discussion in all of the popular gaming forums and subreddits were censored. Mundane Matt made a YouTube video on it. Zoe Quinn or someone claiming to be her issued a false copyright notice/takedown. Adam Baldwin tweeted about that with the hashtag #Gamergate.

That isn't a stupid question. Sometimes we all need a refresher.
A woman had sex with 5 gaming journalists so that they'd give her game good reviews. Her boyfriend got mad and told everyone. That was GamerGate.

One thing that I don't think has been mentioned here yet is that GamerGate as a whole was pretty successful.

A big part of the actual movement was coordinated movements against the specific "news" websites that were propagating the type of crap that the movement was rallying against. This usually took the form of attempting to get sponsors to de-fund these sites. Although this was only nominally successful a handful of times, Gawker's name was dragged through the dirt enough that they lost a TON of money that they probably wouldn't have when the Hulk Hogan scandal drove the nail into their coffin. I mean it was high profile enough that Intel cut their funding. Considering how massive Gawker was beforehand this is a pretty big deal.

It also led to the rapid increase of independent game critics - ones that weren't "e-celebs" like had existed before, but people who spent most of their time just trying to give unbiased reviews of games.

That's the legacy of the movement. The legacy of the scandal isn't quite as picturesque.

The Wikipedia page for Gamergate was, and continues to be, a battleground of truly comical proportions. The talk page is almost as cancerous as the talk page for HAES.

The problem was that Quinn, who started the entire thing, tried to paint a picture of all of gaming coming after her because she was a woman. For the SJW movement (who'd been looking for something to pile on for a long time at that point) she was saying exactly what they wanted to hear, and it turned into a war. The problem is that the SJW movement is quite a bit larger than you'd think it is from Voat or Reddit, and Quinn became a martyr. Now she's giving talks to the UN about how awful it is to live in middle class America.

On the other hand, GamerGate's legacy is also a lot more far-reaching. It made the insanity of the SJW movement WAY more public than it had been at that point, and led to much of Reddit joining the anti-SJW camp. It's highly unlikely that Pao hate would have reached the fever pitch it did if GamerGate hadn't forced it into everyone's eyes. It also opened the floodgates of mod hate in reddit - although frequenters of /r/undelete had long since known of reddit's cancerous upper class, the general reddit public really didn't care...well, until /r/games mods decided to go nuclear about the entire thing and, once again, blow up the formerly small scandal into a redditwide Event^tm .

So in a way, Gamergate is a big part of the reason reddit started to fall apart a couple years ago. It was the spark that lit up a room that had been filling up with gasoline for years.
